title: Exactly Twenty Terms
statement:
A repunit is a positive integer whose decimal digits are all equal to $1$, so the repunits are $1, 11, 111, \dots$.

How many positive integers less than $10^4$ can be written as a sum of exactly $20$ repunits, where the same repunit may be used more than once and the order of the terms does not matter?
hints: Multiply a repunit by $9$ and add $1$. What number do you get? Now see what happens to a sum $N$ of $20$ repunits when you form $9N + 20$.

Since $9R_k + 1 = 10^k$ for the repunit $R_k$ with $k$ digits, the number $Q = \frac{9N+20}{10}$ is a sum of exactly $20$ powers of ten, with exponents at least $0$. Use digit sums to decide which $Q$ can occur: replacing ten copies of a power of ten by the next power is a carry, and it lowers the number of terms by $9$.

With $Q = \frac{9N+20}{10}$, the valid values of $N$ correspond to the integers $Q$ with $20 \le Q \le 9001$ whose digit sum is $2$, $11$ or $20$. Stars and bars with inclusion-exclusion shows that the strings of $4$ digits with these digit sums number $10$, $348$ and $633$ respectively. Now discard the strings whose value lies outside the range.
solution: Let $R_k$ be the repunit with $k$ digits, so $9R_k+1=10^k$. If $N=R_{k_1}+\dots+R_{k_{20}}$ with all $k_i\ge1$, then $$9N+20=10^{k_1}+\dots+10^{k_{20}}.$$ Hence $Q=\frac{9N+20}{10}$ is an integer and a sum of exactly $20$ powers of ten with exponents $\ge0$. Conversely, if $Q=10^{e_1}+\dots+10^{e_{20}}$ with $e_i\ge0$, then $N=R_{e_1+1}+\dots+R_{e_{20}+1}$ satisfies $9N+20=10Q$. So $N\leftrightarrow Q$ is a bijection between the integers $N$ in question and the integers $Q$ that are sums of exactly $20$ powers of ten. Moreover $N\le 9999$ iff $10Q\le 90011$, i.e. $Q\le 9001$. Claim. $Q$ is a sum of exactly $20$ powers of ten iff $Q\ge 20$ and $s(Q)\in\{2,11,20\}$, where $s$ is the digit sum. Proof. Suppose $Q$ is such a sum. Each term is at least $1$, so $Q\ge20$. While some power occurs at least ten times, replace ten copies of it by one copy of the next power. The value is unchanged and the number of terms drops by $9$, so the process ends, with each power occurring at most nine times. This is the decimal expansion of $Q$, so $s(Q)=20-9t$ for some integer $t\ge0$. As $s(Q)>0$, we get $s(Q)\in\{2,11,20\}$. Conversely, let $Q\ge20$ and $s(Q)\in\{2,11,20\}$. The decimal expansion writes $Q$ as a sum of $s(Q)\le 20$ powers of ten. If there are fewer than $20$ terms and all were $1$, the sum would be less than $20$. So some term is at least $10$, and replacing it by ten copies of the next lower power adds $9$ terms. Since $s(Q)\equiv20\pmod 9$, repeating this reaches exactly $20$ terms. $\square$ So we count $Q$ with $20\le Q\le 9001$ and $s(Q)\in\{2,11,20\}$. Consider all $4$-digit strings (representing $0$ to $9999$). By stars and bars with inclusion-exclusion for digits $\ge10$, the numbers of strings with digit sum $2$, $11$, $20$ are $$\binom53=10,\qquad \binom{14}{3}-4\binom43=348,\qquad \binom{23}{3}-4\binom{13}{3}+6\binom33=633,$$ totalling $991$. Remove $Q\ge 9002$. These have first digit $9$ and last three digits forming a number $\ge2$. Digit sum $2$ is impossible. Digit sum $11$ needs the last three digits to sum to $2$, giving $\binom42=6$ strings. Digit sum $20$ needs them to sum to $11$, giving $\binom{13}{2}-3\binom32=69$ strings. All of these have last three digits forming a number $\ge2$, since $000$ and $001$ have digit sums $0$ and $1$. So $75$ are removed. Remove $Q<20$. Numbers below $20$ have digit sum at most $10$, so the only ones with digit sum in $\{2,11,20\}$ are those with digit sum $2$, namely $2$ and $11$. So $2$ are removed. The count is $991-75-2=914$.
